title: From manuscript to printed Bible
scope: Selected histories of European Bible production, Jewish editorial traditions and Massachusett translation and printing, with Asian printing precedence acknowledged. Close investigations of a 1516 primary page, copy-level variation and modern editorial policies; not a global translation census.
thesis: Printing changes the reproduction of books; it does not end textual variation, editing, translation or hand work.

editions.name: The 42-line Bible
editions.people: Johannes Gutenberg’s workshop; financier Johann Fust; Peter Schoeffer; rubricators and binders.
editions.claim: A printed book could still need a hand to finish it.

layers.label: Printed text
layers.title: The press repeats a setting
layers.text: Movable metal type carried a Latin Vulgate text. Two columns resemble manuscript book design. “42-line” names the usual column length, not every page. Printing multiplied an edited exemplar; it did not return directly to the biblical authors.

layers.label: Hand finishing
layers.title: An individual copy emerges
layers.text: Illuminators added decorated initials after printing. Cambridge’s copy preserves this mixture of mechanical reproduction and manual work. Turn this layer off to see why a printed sheet was not necessarily a finished page.

layers.label: Page furniture
layers.title: Instructions could travel with the sheets
layers.text: The Bavarian copy preserves a printed rubrication guide. Rubrics are headings or directions, not a separate biblical witness. This model marks their function without reproducing a particular leaf.

editions.limit: Schematic of a typical two-column page. No original letters, ornament, damage or exact line count is reproduced.

editions.name: The Second Rabbinic Bible
editions.people: Jacob ben Hayyim ibn Adonijah, editor; Daniel Bomberg, printer and publisher.
editions.claim: The margins are part of the reading instrument.

layers.label: Biblical text
layers.title: A selected Masoretic text
layers.text: Ben Hayyim’s edition established an influential printed form of the Hebrew Bible. Hebrew printing was already decades old: the Soncino press had issued a complete Hebrew Bible in 1488.

layers.label: Masorah
layers.title: Notes about transmission
layers.text: Masoretic notes preserve information about the text’s wording and forms. They are distinct from an explanatory commentary and from a modern apparatus that compares witnesses.

layers.label: Targum & commentary
layers.title: Translation and interpretation alongside
layers.text: Aramaic targum and rabbinic commentary surround the biblical text. These are different kinds of writing, not extra Hebrew verses. The schematic groups functions rather than reproducing one book’s exact layout.

editions.limit: The series is commonly dated 1524/25; another holding record gives 1525–26. Dates may describe different components. This is not a collation of a particular set.

editions.name: The Complutensian Polyglot
editions.people: Cardinal Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros, patron; Arnao Guillén de Brocar, printer; Demetrius Ducas and Hebrew scholars including Pablo Coronel and Alfonso de Zamora.
editions.claim: Several columns do not mean several independent originals.

layers.label: Hebrew & Greek
layers.title: Two textual traditions in view
layers.text: The Old Testament places Hebrew beside the Greek Septuagint. The latter is an ancient translation tradition with its own manuscript history. The columns were edited, not simply photographed from ancient books.

layers.label: Latin aids
layers.title: Latin serves more than one purpose
layers.text: The central Vulgate is separate from the Latin aid attached to the Greek. Page design helps a Latin-reading scholar compare languages, but placement also conveys an editorial hierarchy.

layers.label: Targum
layers.title: A Pentateuch-specific lower register
layers.text: In the Pentateuch, the Aramaic Targum Onkelos appears with a Latin translation below the main columns. That layout should not be projected onto every biblical book.

editions.limit: Functional schematic of a Pentateuch page. Column order can vary with the opening; line alignment here does not claim word-for-word equivalence.

editions.name: Novum Instrumentum omne
editions.people: Desiderius Erasmus, editor and Latin translator; Johann Froben, printer.
editions.claim: Editing Greek and translating Latin were distinct tasks in one volume.

layers.label: Greek
layers.title: An edited source-language text
layers.text: Erasmus’s edition made a complete Greek New Testament publicly available in 1516. A limited manuscript supply and rapid production constrained the work. It was revised repeatedly; “Erasmus’s text” is not a single unchanging object.

layers.label: Latin
layers.title: A new rendering for readers
layers.text: The accompanying Latin version expresses Erasmus’s translation decisions. Agreement between two columns on the same printed page is not automatically independent manuscript support.

layers.label: Annotations
layers.title: An argument beyond the opening
layers.text: Erasmus explained decisions in his Annotationes. The band in this diagram represents the separate annotations in the volume, not footnotes physically beneath each Greek page.

editions.limit: Schematic of the volume’s functions, not a facsimile. The annotations band deliberately compresses separate material.

editions.name: Biblia Hebraica Quinta
editions.people: An international editorial team; German Bible Society. Adrian Schenker led the project’s earlier phase.
editions.claim: A diplomatic text can accompany active textual criticism.

layers.label: Base text
layers.title: Print a particular witness
layers.text: BHQ presents the Leningrad Codex (EBP. I B 19a) as its base. “Diplomatic” means representing that witness; it does not mean declaring every reading the earliest recoverable form.

layers.label: Masorah
layers.title: Retain the scribal apparatus
layers.text: Both the small and large Masorah belong to the manuscript tradition being edited. Keeping them visible preserves information a bare consonantal text would lose.

layers.label: Critical apparatus
layers.title: Compare beyond the base
layers.text: Other Hebrew witnesses and ancient versions enter the apparatus and commentary. An editor can discuss a preferable reading without silently replacing the manuscript text printed above.

editions.limit: BHQ is issued in fascicles. This is a functional model, not a reproduction of a copyrighted page or a claim that the whole project is complete.

editions.name: Novum Testamentum Graece
editions.people: The Nestle–Aland editorial tradition, INTF researchers and an international committee; German Bible Society.
editions.claim: The main text is an editorial judgment, not one copied codex.

layers.label: Edited text
layers.title: Reconstruct across witnesses
layers.text: The Greek reading text results from comparing evidence. Unlike BHQ’s base-text policy, it is not a diplomatic reproduction of one manuscript. Neither approach removes the need for judgment.

layers.label: References
layers.title: Connections are not variants
layers.text: Marginal references lead to related passages. They perform a different job from the apparatus below the text: a cross-reference is not a vote for a textual reading.

layers.label: Critical apparatus
layers.title: Make alternatives inspectable
layers.text: NA28 incorporated ECM decisions in the Catholic Letters, James through Jude. The publisher identifies Jude 5 among meaningful textual changes. Even a mature printed edition can revise its main text.

editions.limit: NA28 is used here as a dated case study, not as a permanent “latest edition.” The publisher’s NA29 notice describes further work in preparation.

networks.title: Hebrew editions
networks.intro: Follow BHQ back to its manuscript base and its predecessors. Editorial succession and textual basis are different relationships.

nodes.label: Ben Hayyim
nodes.note: A printed Masoretic text edited for Bomberg’s Second Rabbinic Bible.

nodes.label: BHK 1–2
nodes.note: Kittel used Ben Hayyim’s text, adding a critical apparatus.

nodes.label: Leningrad Codex
nodes.note: A manuscript witness. The Society dates it 1008; 1008/09 is also used in cataloguing.

nodes.label: BHK 3
nodes.note: Paul Kahle helped secure the change to a manuscript base.

nodes.label: BHS
nodes.note: Elliger and Rudolph’s edition; Masorah work by Gérard E. Weil.

nodes.label: BHQ
nodes.note: New apparatus and commentary, retaining Leningrad as base.

networks.limit: No direct copying line from Ben Hayyim to the Leningrad Codex is claimed. Ancient versions and additional Hebrew witnesses also inform the apparatus; they are not all drawn.

networks.title: Early Greek editions
networks.intro: Printed predecessors, manuscript variants and editorial revision meet. Select a node to see the precise relationships supported by the sources.

nodes.label: Erasmus editions
nodes.note: Multiple editions, not one fixed text. The first two lack the Comma; the third includes it.

nodes.label: Complutensian
nodes.note: Independent production at Alcalá; circulation later than its printing date.

nodes.label: Estienne / Stephanus
nodes.note: An influential edition with marginal variants. The source account connects his work with Erasmus and the Complutensian.

nodes.label: Codex Bezae
nodes.note: A Greek–Latin manuscript. Citing a reading does not mean adopting its entire text.

nodes.label: Beza’s editions
nodes.note: Beza used textual variants collected by Robert and Henri Estienne.

networks.limit: A selective evidence network, not a manuscript stemma. “Textus Receptus,” associated with the Elzevirs’ 1633 wording, names a printed tradition with differences, not a unique ancient manuscript.

networks.title: Modern Greek editions
networks.intro: Nestle’s first edition combined published scholarship. Later editorial work returned to the witnesses and changed both the apparatus and the reading text.

nodes.label: Tischendorf
nodes.note: One of the three editions compared by Eberhard Nestle.

nodes.label: Westcott & Hort
nodes.note: Another of Nestle’s three inputs, not the sole ancestor of the later edition.

nodes.label: Weymouth
nodes.note: Replaced by Bernhard Weiss’s edition in Nestle’s comparison in 1901.

nodes.label: Nestle
nodes.note: Adopted the reading shared by two of his three edition inputs and recorded the alternative.

nodes.label: ECM
nodes.note: Extensive collations and editorial assessment, using CBGM for relevant work.

nodes.label: NA28
nodes.note: A later member of a repeatedly revised series; ECM affected James–Jude here.

networks.limit: The gap from 1898 to 2012 contains substantial revision, not a direct reprint. Manuscript discoveries, collation and human judgment cannot be reduced to one ancestry line.

translations.name: Luther’s German New Testament
translations.decision: Render the text in idiomatic German
translations.text: The September Testament joined a source-text choice to a vernacular translation project. Its publication date dates that German edition, not the Greek manuscripts behind it.

translations.name: Tyndale’s English New Testament
translations.source: Greek scholarship and earlier translation work
translations.decision: Translate and then revise English wording
translations.production: Cologne attempt interrupted; complete edition printed at Worms
translations.text: The surviving printing history includes failure, relocation and revision. A translation’s later printing can contain editorial changes as well as typesetting differences.

translations.name: Coverdale’s complete English Bible
translations.text: A translation can work through other translations. “First complete printed English Bible” does not mean “first English Bible” or direct translation throughout from Hebrew and Greek.

translations.name: Rheims New Testament
translations.decision: Gregory Martin’s English rendering, reviewed by colleagues
translations.text: A Catholic translation project chose a different source-text policy from many Protestant projects. Confessional commitments affected the work, but its evidence must still be assessed passage by passage.

translations.name: King James Bible
translations.source: Bishops’ Bible as English revision base; earlier versions consulted
translations.text: The English revision base must not be confused with a single Hebrew or Greek edition. The project combined linguistic scholarship, inherited English phrasing and collective review.

teachingSequence.title: Make and compare copies
teachingSequence.outcome: Explain why repeatable type can still produce different copies.

teachingSequence.title: Read the architecture
teachingSequence.outcome: Distinguish biblical text, Masorah, commentary, translation and apparatus.

teachingSequence.title: Trace documented inputs
teachingSequence.outcome: Follow multiple kinds of relationship without inventing one chain.

teachingSequence.title: Inspect a real page and test an argument
teachingSequence.outcome: Read 1516 evidence before assessing the 1522 revision and promise story.

teachingSequence.title: Separate translation from production
teachingSequence.outcome: Recognize language choices, collaborative work and changing readerships.

teachingSequence.title: Read beneath the line
teachingSequence.outcome: Compare diplomatic, eclectic and synoptic aims and see why modern editions keep changing.

anchors.claim: Parchment preparation, ruling, copying, illumination and binding were distinguishable tasks; skilled hand work continued after print.

Plantin obtained type from specialists including Claude Garamond, Guillaume Le Bé and Robert Granjon. Punches and matrices enabled casting; compositors arranged type and proofreaders checked impressions. The interactive PRNIT/PRINT exercise is invented to demonstrate repeated settings and corrected states.
anchors.limit: No numerical model of historical production rates; no invented Bible reading.

anchors.claim: Movable type in Asia precedes Gutenberg; the European printing story is not a global invention claim.
The Soncino family’s complete printed Hebrew Bible appeared in 1488; Hebrew printing is not merely a preliminary stage of Christian editions.

Complutensian colophons date NT printing to 10 January 1514, reference volume to 17 March 1515 and OT to 10 July 1517. Authorization is dated 22 March 1520. Circulation circa 1522 is less firmly pinned down.

Plantin’s Antwerp project was directed by Arias Montanus with Philip II’s support; museum describes eight volumes and five languages. Its account-book record dates the production programme 1568–73; individual imprints are often dated 1569–72.
anchors.limit: No claim that every passage appears in every language; dates of project, volumes and release differ.

anchors.claim: Brian Walton’s London Polyglot, 1654–57, used subscription funding and brought together more versions. Six volumes; its nine-language range is not nine versions of every biblical book.
anchors.limit: A selection from the polyglot tradition; Paris Polyglot (1628–45) acknowledged but not reconstructed here.

anchors.claim: The Comma Johanneum is absent from Erasmus’s Greek editions of 1516 and 1519 and included in 1522.

De Jonge rejects the traditional promise story after examining the retrospective conditional in Erasmus’s reply to Edward Lee. A theory of motivation must not be presented as if it were a colophon fact.
anchors.limit: Do not infer the text’s earliest form merely by voting among printed editions. Do not repeat unsupported claims that a manuscript was demonstrably manufactured to force a promise.

anchors.claim: Tregelles’s introduction discusses Erasmus’s treatment of the ending. Further direct comparison of the 1516 edition and its manuscript is needed for a detailed on-page case study.
anchors.publication: Not used for a word-level reconstruction in this study.

anchors.claim: John Mill’s 1707 Greek Testament assembled variant readings after decades of work, helping separate inherited printed text from evidence collected below it.
anchors.limit: No unsupported precise variant count is used.

anchors.classification: methodological interpretation grounded in project documentation
anchors.claim: CBGM helps assess relations among witness texts and local variant relationships. It does not eliminate editorial judgment or simply trace the physical parentage of codices.
NA28’s publisher identifies meaningful main-text revision in the Catholic Letters through ECM work, with Jude 5 as an example. No full copyrighted apparatus reproduced.
BHQ continues in fascicles. The NA29 project notice describes work in preparation including ECM developments in Mark, Acts and Revelation.
anchors.limit: Status is attributed to the publisher as checked 2026-10-13, not a promise of a release date.

anchors.claim: The Septuagint has its own edition history. Rahlfs’s compact 1935 edition was revised by Hanhart in 2006. The larger Göttingen series publishes individual books with named editors, including John William Wevers’s Genesis (1974).
anchors.limit: Do not confuse the Septuagint project’s large critical edition with the INTF Greek New Testament ECM. No simple succession chain between the compact edition and every Göttingen volume is implied.

disagreementsAndLimits.resolution: Qualify first printed versus first published; qualify complete Bible versus NT; qualify language and geography. Gutenberg did not invent all printing.
Only draw listed documented relationships. Solid = textual basis/influence; dotted = collation; dashed = editorial succession. Connections do not mean identity of every reading or exclusive descent.
Historical prefaces may defend a hierarchy of languages or versions. Describe those commitments as their authors’ interpretations, not neutral facts about the intrinsic value of a language.
A retrospective label for related printed Greek editions; not one manuscript or an invariant text. Hebrew use of received-text terminology is a separate history.
Different editorial aims. A diplomatic edition can have a critically evaluative apparatus; an eclectic text does not have to follow whichever witness is oldest or most numerous.
Even institutions disagree. Retain Bomberg dating variations and Antwerp project/imprint distinctions. Reject Newberry’s internally inconsistent Antwerp totals in favor of the holding museum.
Silence in a selective apparatus does not establish that all witnesses agree; Habakkuk 3:1 is a comparison of editorial reporting.
Avoid attributing the whole Massachusett Bible to an isolated European translator or treating colonial literacy as uncomplicated progress.

artwork.rights: Basel e-rara page Public Domain Mark; other graphics are original teaching schematics.
artwork.limits: Schematics are labelled. Greek and Hebrew excerpts are short normalized transcriptions; no full modern apparatus reproduced. The press exercise is invented.

deeperReading.readStatus: Article read; original replies accessed through its quotations.

deeperReading.purpose: A longer social history of the Comma dispute, connecting textual decisions with confessional controversy.
deeperReading.readStatus: Publisher description and contents only; full monograph not read.

deeperReading.purpose: A worked critique of compact apparatuses, using Habakkuk; argues for seeing witnesses in context.
deeperReading.readStatus: Edition-method and Habakkuk sections read. This is an argued position, not a consensus statement.

deeperReading.purpose: Read the editors’ case for reconstructed Hebrew texts and parallel ancient editions.
deeperReading.readStatus: Project statement reviewed; full critical volumes not read.

deeperReading.purpose: A continuing Jewish edition of text, Masorah, targum and commentary grounded in manuscript research.
Follow individual copies beyond the publication date through a specialist census.
deeperReading.readStatus: Project introduction located; census entries not audited.

deeperReading.purpose: Understand how textual relationships inform modern editing without becoming a family tree of physical books.

Keep translation, source-text editing and reproduction technology analytically distinct.

caseStudies.question: Can two copies of the same edition differ?
caseStudies.observed: Agata’s image comparison detected changes within settings, including type orientation, spelling and punctuation.
caseStudies.inferred: Ordering corrected and uncorrected states can reconstruct production, but a bound copy can mix states of different sheets.
caseStudies.teachingModel: Existing PRNIT/PRINT setting exercise retained; fictional word expressly labelled. No historical Bible variant is simulated as real.
caseStudies.limit: Published summary examined; full collation tables not inspected.

caseStudies.question: What can a printed page establish?
caseStudies.object: Basel UBH BibG B 3, Novum Instrumentum (1516), printed p. 183, IIIF canvas 896099.
caseStudies.observed: Greek in left column, Latin in right. At 1 John 5:7–8 the list is spirit, water, blood without the heavenly witnesses clause. Chapter V appears in Latin margin; bottom has signature q3 and a catchword.

transcription.greek: τὸ πνεῦμα, καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ καὶ τὸ αἷμα
transcription.english: the spirit, and the water and the blood
transcription.method: Short normalized Greek excerpt: abbreviations expanded, typography and punctuation normalized. English is a literal study rendering, not a complete verse translation.

caseStudies.inferred: The two columns belong to one editorial project and cannot be counted as two independent ancient manuscript votes.
caseStudies.limit: 1519/1522 states are supported by research; only 1516 page directly inspected here. Handwritten marginal note is not dated or attributed.

caseStudies.question: Does Erasmus’s reply promise a future insertion?
caseStudies.primaryLocator: Responsio ad Annotationes Eduardi Lei (May 1520), Clericus IX, col. 275 BC, quoted by de Jonge p. 385.
caseStudies.rendering: If a single copy had come into my hands
caseStudies.observed: The quoted Latin uses an unreal past condition; the continuation explains what Erasmus would have done.
caseStudies.interpretation: De Jonge challenges the promise anecdote and reads the reply as a defense of earlier editions. Theological pressure and publishing aims matter, but motives remain argued interpretations.
caseStudies.limit: This is a quotation through modern research, not a direct examination of the 1520 printing. No claim that a codex was proved manufactured to force a promise.

caseStudies.question: Does a revised apparatus require a revised main text?
caseStudies.observed: Prinsloo reports no BHS note at this phrase, but a BHQ note recording omission of “the prophet” in the Barberini Greek version.
caseStudies.interpretation: A reader gains a comparison without losing the diplomatic base text. Absence of an apparatus entry does not prove universal agreement.
caseStudies.limit: Normalized phrase and paraphrased comparison, not a facsimile or complete apparatus. No independent collation of Barberini or the two printed editions.

caseStudies.question: What is the main text trying to represent?

positions.name: BHQ
positions.aim: Document Leningrad as a stable reference, critically evaluate variants in apparatus/commentary.

positions.name: HBCE
positions.aim: Reconstruct earliest inferable textual forms; separate columns where ancient editions differ.

positions.name: Synoptic proposal
positions.aim: Prinsloo argues for contextual comparison of witness texts so compact apparatuses do not conceal assumptions.

caseStudies.interpretation: Different answers make different research tools. Diplomatic does not mean uncritical, and a reconstructed archetype does not mean an author’s autograph.
caseStudies.limit: The reconstruction debate is substantial; the synoptic proposal is an attributed argument, not the replacement consensus.

caseStudies.question: Whose work disappears from a book’s familiar name?
caseStudies.observed: Bridwell’s 1685 revised Eliot Bible record names Job Nesutan and James Printer; Peabody identifies Printer as Nipmuc and documents his typesetting.
caseStudies.interpretation: Translation, composition and correction could overlap in one skilled person while remaining distinct tasks. Missionary publication and later Indigenous language reclamation give the same text different purposes.
caseStudies.limit: No exact distribution of translated passages among collaborators reconstructed. No exclusive Geneva/KJV base asserted. Excavated type belongs to broader press history, not automatically to this Bible.
